Professor Dorothy Yeboah-Manu is a Ghanaian medical microbiologist, biomedical researcher and academic whose work has contributed significantly to the study of tuberculosis, Buruli ulcer and other infectious diseases.
She is the first woman to serve as Director of the Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research at the University of Ghana. Her career combines laboratory research, public health, academic leadership and the training of scientists across Ghana and Africa.
Education and Training
Professor Yeboah-Manu began her university education at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, where she graduated with a First Class Bachelor of Science degree in Biochemistry.
She later obtained a Master’s degree in Applied Molecular Biology of Infectious Diseases from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine in the United Kingdom.
She completed her PhD in Microbiology at the Swiss Tropical and Public Health Institute of the University of Basel in Switzerland in 2006.
Her training exposed her to modern approaches in molecular biology, microbiology, genetics, infectious disease research and pathogen surveillance.
Career at Noguchi Memorial Institute
Professor Yeboah-Manu joined the Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research as a research assistant and gradually rose through the ranks.

# Professor Dorothy Yeboah-Manu is a... - Charles Wundengba | Facebook
## Charles Wundengba's Post
She has served as a research fellow, senior research fellow, head of the Department of Bacteriology and Deputy Director of the West African Centre for Cell Biology of Infectious Pathogens.
She became Director of the Noguchi Memorial Institute, where she leads one of Ghana’s most important biomedical research institutions.
Under her leadership, the Institute continues to conduct research into infectious and non-communicable diseases, strengthen laboratory capacity, train researchers and support national responses to public health emergencies.
Research on Tuberculosis
One of Professor Yeboah-Manu’s major areas of research is tuberculosis.
Her work includes the study of the biology, genetics, transmission patterns and drug resistance of tuberculosis-causing bacteria. She has also contributed to research on Mycobacterium africanum, a tuberculosis pathogen associated particularly with West Africa.
Her research has helped improve understanding of how tuberculosis spreads and how genetic differences among bacteria may affect diagnosis, treatment and disease control.
She has also worked on the relationship between tuberculosis and other health conditions, including type 2 diabetes.
Professor Yeboah-Manu is involved in African research collaborations studying drug-resistant tuberculosis, pathogen genomics and transmission dynamics. These studies are important because drug-resistant tuberculosis remains a serious threat to public health.
Research on Buruli Ulcer
Another important part of her scientific work concerns Buruli ulcer, a neglected tropical disease caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans.
Buruli ulcer can cause severe skin damage, disability and long-term social difficulties if it is not diagnosed and treated early. The disease often affects people in rural communities where access to specialised health services may be limited.
Professor Yeboah-Manu was part of a research team that identified genetic markers used to study Mycobacterium ulcerans isolates from Ghana. The team’s findings demonstrated genetic diversity among African strains, challenging the earlier belief that African isolates were largely identical.
Her work has also contributed to improving diagnosis and understanding the epidemiology of Buruli ulcer.
Leadership and Mentorship
Professor Yeboah-Manu has played a major role in building scientific capacity in Ghana and Africa.
She has helped develop research programmes, supervise students and mentor early-career scientists. She has also supported initiatives designed to increase the number of women participating in biomedical research.

# Professor Dorothy Yeboah-Manu is a... - Charles Wundengba | Facebook
## Charles Wundengba's Post
She is associated with the TALENT programme, an all-female West African PhD initiative intended to help reduce the gender gap in scientific research and leadership.
Professional Service
Professor Yeboah-Manu is a member of several international and national scientific organisations.
Her professional affiliations include the American Society for Microbiology, the International Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease, the World Health Organization’s Global Network of Laboratories Confirming Buruli Ulcer and the Federation of African Immunological Societies.
She is also Chairperson of the Advisory Board of Ghana’s National Tuberculosis Control Programme.
She has served on research committees, scientific advisory bodies and boards supporting infectious disease research and public health policy.
Awards and Recognition
In 2018, Professor Yeboah-Manu received the Royal Society Africa Prize. The award recognised her innovative contribution to the understanding of the microbiology, genetics and molecular epidemiology of Mycobacterium ulcerans and Mycobacterium africanum.
She is also a Fellow of the Ghana Academy of Arts and Sciences and a Senior Fellow of the European and Developing Countries Clinical Trials Partnership.
Her work has attracted support from organisations including the Wellcome Trust and other international research and development institutions.
The University of Ghana’s research platform lists hundreds of publications connected to her work and records a substantial citation and research impact profile.
Contribution to Ghana
Professor Yeboah-Manu’s contribution is important because much of her research focuses on diseases that directly affect African populations.
Rather than relying entirely on research conducted outside the continent, her work helps generate local evidence about the bacteria, disease patterns and treatment challenges found in Ghana and West Africa.
Her research supports better diagnosis, disease surveillance, public health planning and scientific training.
She has also helped demonstrate that Ghanaian scientists can lead internationally respected research programmes while building institutions and mentoring the next generation at home.

## 4 Discussion
Evidence on the association between diabetes and TB clinical presentation is mixed. In our cohort, TB-diabetes participants had fewer pulmonary cavities. This is consistent with a previous study, but contrasts with most reports, including the previous Ghana study (12), which reported higher cavitation. A few others found no difference (29, 35). Previous research shows that glycaemic control is more closely linked to radiographic severity than diabetes status alone, with poor control associated with more extensive cavitation (24). In our study, most TB–diabetes participants were newly diagnosed, which may have meant shorter diabetes duration. Also, although many previously diagnosed participants had poor glycaemic control they were receiving metformin. Metformin may reduce lung damage through immune modulation, enhanced autophagy, and inhibition of matrix metalloproteinases (36–39). Cavitation also varies by age and sex, with higher prevalence in males and lower prevalence in older patients (24). In our study, the TB–diabetes group had fewer males and were older on average, which may have contributed to the lower cavitation prevalence observed. Because pulmonary cavitation is a hallmark of PTB (40), its reduced frequency in patients with diabetes warrants caution in settings that rely heavily on clinical or radiographic features for diagnosis. Larger studies are needed to confirm our findings and better define the influence of diabetes severity, treatment, and patient characteristics on radiographic manifestations of pulmonary TB.
texts.29:
## 4 Discussion
Contrary to some studies reporting an association between diabetes and unfavorable TB outcomes (3–5, 12, 41), we observed no significant differences in treatment outcomes by diabetes status. Month 2 sputum smear positivity, a known predictor of unfavorable outcomes (42), was also similar between groups and less frequent among TB-diabetes participants. Possible explanations for these findings include metformin use among some TB–diabetes participants and the high proportion of newly diagnosed cases. Metformin, beyond reducing lung damage, has been associated with reduced TB mortality (43) and improved treatment outcomes, including faster sputum conversion (44). In addition, it appears that many newly diagnosed participants had transient hyperglycaemia, with glucose normalizing with TB treatment. Transient hyperglycaemia has been associated with unfavorable TB outcomes in some settings (45, 46). However, this did not translate into unfavorable outcomes in our cohort. Furthermore, the lower prevalence of pulmonary cavitation among TB-diabetes participants may have further mitigated unfavorable outcomes. Cavitation has been shown to be a stronger predictor of unfavorable treatment outcomes than diabetes itself (47). Nevertheless, larger longitudinal studies are needed to confirm these findings and explain the underlying mechanisms.
This study has limitations. We did not use the oral glucose tolerance test, the diagnostic gold standard for diabetes, which may have resulted in missed cases. However, the combined use of FPG and HbA1c, both recommended for diabetes screening in TB patients (34), is expected to enhance diagnostic sensitivity. Mycobacterial clearance was assessed by sputum smear rather than culture, potentially underestimating persistent infection. Some participants missed scheduled glucose testing during TB treatment, limiting longitudinal data on glycaemic variability. Few participants with previously diagnosed diabetes constrained evaluation of glucose control in relation to TB outcomes. Limited diabetes management data precluded comprehensive assessment of treatment effects.
Despite these limitations, our findings support integrating diabetes screening into TB services in the Greater Accra Region to enable early detection and strengthen health system responses to the dual burden of communicable and non-communicable diseases. Further research is needed to identify effective strategies for integrating diabetes screening and care into routine TB services. In addition, larger studies in this setting incorporating comprehensive longitudinal monitoring of glycaemic variability, detailed diabetes management data, measures of diabetes severity, pharmacologic information, and relevant biomarkers are needed to clarify the impact of diabetes on TB presentation and treatment outcomes.

Professor Dorothy Yeboah-Manu is a Ghanaian medical microbiologist, biomedical researcher and academic whose work has contributed significantly to the study of tuberculosis, Buruli ulcer and other infectious diseases.
She is the first woman to serve as Director of the Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research at the University of Ghana. Her career combines laboratory research, public health, academic leadership and the training of scientists across Ghana and Africa.
Education and Training
Professor Yeboah-Manu began her university education at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, where she graduated with a First Class Bachelor of Science degree in Biochemistry.
She later obtained a Master’s degree in Applied Molecular Biology of Infectious Diseases from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine in the United Kingdom.
She completed her PhD in Microbiology at the Swiss Tropical and Public Health Institute of the University of Basel in Switzerland in 2006.
Her training exposed her to modern approaches in molecular biology, microbiology, genetics, infectious disease research and pathogen surveillance.
Career at Noguchi Memorial Institute
Professor Yeboah-Manu joined the Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research as a research assistant and gradually rose through the ranks.

# Professor Dorothy Yeboah-Manu is a... - Charles Wundengba | Facebook
## Charles Wundengba's Post
She has served as a research fellow, senior research fellow, head of the Department of Bacteriology and Deputy Director of the West African Centre for Cell Biology of Infectious Pathogens.
She became Director of the Noguchi Memorial Institute, where she leads one of Ghana’s most important biomedical research institutions.
Under her leadership, the Institute continues to conduct research into infectious and non-communicable diseases, strengthen laboratory capacity, train researchers and support national responses to public health emergencies.
Research on Tuberculosis
One of Professor Yeboah-Manu’s major areas of research is tuberculosis.
Her work includes the study of the biology, genetics, transmission patterns and drug resistance of tuberculosis-causing bacteria. She has also contributed to research on Mycobacterium africanum, a tuberculosis pathogen associated particularly with West Africa.
Her research has helped improve understanding of how tuberculosis spreads and how genetic differences among bacteria may affect diagnosis, treatment and disease control.
She has also worked on the relationship between tuberculosis and other health conditions, including type 2 diabetes.
Professor Yeboah-Manu is involved in African research collaborations studying drug-resistant tuberculosis, pathogen genomics and transmission dynamics. These studies are important because drug-resistant tuberculosis remains a serious threat to public health.
Research on Buruli Ulcer
Another important part of her scientific work concerns Buruli ulcer, a neglected tropical disease caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans.
Buruli ulcer can cause severe skin damage, disability and long-term social difficulties if it is not diagnosed and treated early. The disease often affects people in rural communities where access to specialised health services may be limited.
Professor Yeboah-Manu was part of a research team that identified genetic markers used to study Mycobacterium ulcerans isolates from Ghana. The team’s findings demonstrated genetic diversity among African strains, challenging the earlier belief that African isolates were largely identical.
Her work has also contributed to improving diagnosis and understanding the epidemiology of Buruli ulcer.
Leadership and Mentorship
Professor Yeboah-Manu has played a major role in building scientific capacity in Ghana and Africa.
She has helped develop research programmes, supervise students and mentor early-career scientists. She has also supported initiatives designed to increase the number of women participating in biomedical research.

# Professor Dorothy Yeboah-Manu is a... - Charles Wundengba | Facebook
## Charles Wundengba's Post
She is associated with the TALENT programme, an all-female West African PhD initiative intended to help reduce the gender gap in scientific research and leadership.
Professional Service
Professor Yeboah-Manu is a member of several international and national scientific organisations.
Her professional affiliations include the American Society for Microbiology, the International Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease, the World Health Organization’s Global Network of Laboratories Confirming Buruli Ulcer and the Federation of African Immunological Societies.
She is also Chairperson of the Advisory Board of Ghana’s National Tuberculosis Control Programme.
She has served on research committees, scientific advisory bodies and boards supporting infectious disease research and public health policy.
Awards and Recognition
In 2018, Professor Yeboah-Manu received the Royal Society Africa Prize. The award recognised her innovative contribution to the understanding of the microbiology, genetics and molecular epidemiology of Mycobacterium ulcerans and Mycobacterium africanum.
She is also a Fellow of the Ghana Academy of Arts and Sciences and a Senior Fellow of the European and Developing Countries Clinical Trials Partnership.
Her work has attracted support from organisations including the Wellcome Trust and other international research and development institutions.
The University of Ghana’s research platform lists hundreds of publications connected to her work and records a substantial citation and research impact profile.
Contribution to Ghana
Professor Yeboah-Manu’s contribution is important because much of her research focuses on diseases that directly affect African populations.
Rather than relying entirely on research conducted outside the continent, her work helps generate local evidence about the bacteria, disease patterns and treatment challenges found in Ghana and West Africa.
Her research supports better diagnosis, disease surveillance, public health planning and scientific training.
She has also helped demonstrate that Ghanaian scientists can lead internationally respected research programmes while building institutions and mentoring the next generation at home.
Sources: the Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research, the University of Ghana, the Ghana Academy of Arts and Sciences, the European and Developing Countries Clinical Trials Partnership and the Royal Society.
